title: Important Status Information Is Buried
excerpt: Important status information is buried when information that would change what the user does next is visible but not visually prominent enough for its operational significance. The failure concerns prominence, not presence.
metaDescription: A state visibility failure where important visible information lacks enough visual prominence for users to notice it under operational conditions.
summary: This failure occurs when an interface presents operationally unequal information with equal visual weight. Users can technically see the status, alert, or value, but the display does not make it stand out enough for time-pressured, physically constrained, or attentionally divided use.
definition: Important status information is buried when present, accessible status information is assigned insufficient visual prominence relative to its operational significance, so users can miss it at the moment it should guide action.
keyFacts: This failure concerns visual prominence, not information absence.
The information that matters is visible, but it does not assert itself with the urgency its operational significance warrants.
Uniform visual treatment can make critical alerts, calibration states, and secondary parameters read as equivalent.
Category-based organisation can force users to translate from system categories to operational significance during use.
Static hierarchy can fail when the significance of readings, alerts, or sensor states changes with context.

bodyMarkdown:
## Summary

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Important status information is buried when the interface shows information that would change what the user does next, but gives it insufficient visual prominence for the conditions of use. The information is present. The failure is that the visual hierarchy does not match the operational hierarchy.

This failure appears in complex operational systems where some states demand immediate attention, some are secondary reference, and some are contextual background. If all of them are presented at equal visual weight, the interface implicitly communicates that all of them matter equally. Under time pressure, movement, poor lighting, distance, gloves, or divided attention, users cannot reliably apply deliberate parsing before acting.

## Failure pattern: present status does not stand out as operationally significant

Important status information is buried when the operator can technically read the status, value, alert, or condition, but the interface does not make it prominent enough to be noticed at the moment of use. A calibration fault can sit beside secondary parameters with the same visual weight. An operational alert can receive the same treatment as a minor notification. A retained target can keep the same marker treatment as an updating one.

The failure often looks like user error after the event. A status condition was visible in retrospect, but it was not perceived at the operationally relevant moment. A technician repeats a measurement because the measurement state was not clear enough at working distance. An alert escalates before it is addressed because it did not visually distinguish itself from lower-priority notifications.

The design issue is not user inattentiveness. The interface has placed equal attention demands on unequal information.

## Boundary with absent state visibility and unclear mode changes

This failure is distinct from the failure in which users cannot see what state the system is in. In that adjacent state visibility failure, the state information is absent or not directly accessible, so users must reconstruct or infer what the system is doing. In buried-status failures, the user looking at the display can see the value or condition, but the display does not make it prominent enough for operational use.

This failure is also distinct from unclear mode changes. Mode-change failures concern transitions: the interface fails to communicate when the system moves between modes. Buried-status failures concern continuous display: the interface presents a status accurately and continuously, but at an insufficient level of visual prominence for reliable noticing under operational conditions.

The distinction matters because the design responses differ. Absent state information requires making information present. Unclear mode changes require making transitions legible. Buried status requires making present information structurally assertive.

## Causes: visual hierarchy diverges from operational hierarchy

Equal visual weight assigned to unequal significance is the most direct cause of buried status. Teams often design screens to be complete, consistent, and informative. Those goals can produce visual uniformity. Uniformity removes hierarchy, so the most operationally significant value on the screen becomes visually indistinguishable from the least significant value.

Category-based organisation is another cause. Complex systems are often organised by what values are: engine parameters, alarm states, configuration values, measurement values, or sensor states. Users, however, are often trying to answer a different question: what needs attention now? A category-based display can require the user to translate from system structure to operational significance during every scan.

Static visual hierarchy also fails when significance changes with context. A temperature reading may be secondary during normal operation and critical near a threshold. A low-priority notification may be informational, while a condition affecting primary system function may require immediate response. If both use the same alert treatment, the display does not support rapid priority judgement.

## Beissbarth automotive calibration: measurement state at working distance

In the Beissbarth automotive calibration engagement, calibration equipment was used across three device classes in manufacturer-authorised inspection centres: an embedded OEM display, a rugged tablet, and a large inspection line display. The calibration sequence was sensitive to timing. Technicians moved around the vehicle, read the OEM display from two to three metres, wore gloves that restricted fine touch interaction, and worked in variable lighting that reduced contrast.

The previous interface presented measurement values, tolerances, and progress indicators at equal visual weight across all three device classes. That hierarchy was designed for seated, close-range evaluation, not for workshop use. At two to three metres, while moving, the technician had to distinguish whether a measurement was complete, whether a reading was within tolerance, and whether the next step was safe to proceed from. The visually uniform field did not support that confirmation without deliberate, closer attention.

Creative Navy-recorded work in the Sandbox Experiments phase documented the operational conditions at the level of individual task steps. A twelve-feature, four-module analysis recorded expected technician movement, typical lighting conditions, and acceptable time for state confirmation for each feature. This made the hierarchy issue specific: at the steps where measurement state had to be confirmed from distance, the display's visual organisation did not support single-glance confirmation under the relevant conditions.

Option space mapping produced three structural variants for the OEM display, evaluated under reproduced workshop lighting and viewing distances. Tension-driven reasoning led to a competitive vector that prioritised unambiguous state communication over information density across all three device classes. The redesign accepted reduced information visible at any one moment in exchange for a single reading logic across the system.

Beissbarth client-measured calibration time reduced from 18 minutes to 12 minutes per vehicle across 8 production deployment locations. Repeated measurements reduced directionally, client-measured; the exact figure was not shared. Beissbarth client-reported that the system is now deployed without onboarding training. The reduced measurement error risk is inferred from the design change and the mechanism it addressed, not independently measured as a separate outcome.

## Elsner Cala Touch KNX: alert hierarchy in an embedded controller

The Elsner Elektronik Cala Touch KNX is a wall-mounted smart home and building automation controller installed at 140cm and used approximately 25 times per day in residential settings, commercial offices, and industrial buildings. The device manages heating, cooling, lighting, blinds, and scenes, and receives status inputs from weather stations, CO2 sensors, humidity sensors, temperature probes, and the main heating unit.

Alert conditions in the Cala Touch KNX context had different operational significance. A heating unit alert affected the primary function of the environmental control system and required attention. An open window detection notification was informational and less urgent. Presenting both at the same visual prominence made each alert require investigation before the user could know whether it required action.

Creative Navy's design work introduced a dual-priority alert hierarchy. Heating unit alerts and conditions affecting primary system function were treated as primary signals in the visual hierarchy. Minor notifications, including open window detection and informational status changes, remained present and accessible but did not compete visually with conditions requiring immediate attention.

The sensor state design applied the same principle to delayed sensor readings, contradictory values, and calibration faults. These states were given named representations at appropriate hierarchy levels: present, legible, clearly labelled, and calibrated to significance rather than shown with uniform prominence.

A formal usability test with 12 subjects confirmed that navigation and temperature comprehension met the requirements of the interface under the conditions of use. Touch target sizing was grounded in published ergonomics research applied in formal testing for standing-height use. The alert hierarchy outcomes are limited to design confirmation in prototype testing with Elsner's engineers and were not independently quantified in post-deployment user measurement.

## Additional evidence: maritime VTS, industrial audit findings, and Assemblio

A European vendor of maritime traffic monitoring, inland navigation and communications software for port authorities, coastal administrations and waterway operators showed another form of buried status in Vessel Traffic Services. Time of last observation sat behind secondary inspection. In a degraded state, a retained target could keep the same visual treatment as an updating one, so the display did not reliably tell the operator whether a marker represented a current observation or a last known position. An equipment view with no state data could read as an equipment view with no faults.

In a counterbalanced paired study with eight professional VTS operators and supervisors, each completing four matched tasks in both the existing interface and the redesigned prototype, median time to first answer fell by 42.3% on vessel identification, 34.2% on alert prioritisation and 32.2% on handover retrieval; correct first answers rose from 23 of 32 to 32 of 32; and correct recognition of historical replay rose from 5 of 8 to 8 of 8. This result is Creative Navy-measured under controlled conditions. Eight participants completed four of the seven operator journeys using sanitised training scenarios on a design prototype, not a production installation. Six of the eight had taken part in earlier research or testing. The time measure is time to a first submitted answer regardless of whether that answer was correct, not time to successful completion. The study reports no significance test, no confidence interval and no power calculation, and states that the three percentages must not be combined into one figure. Field observation happened in operational VTS control rooms at a customer site, using sanitised scenarios rather than live traffic.

In an audit for a European industrial automation vendor whose process control software coordinates machining cells, the product in development showed status inconsistency across panels of the same type. Detail cards ran 40–85% empty beside unpaginated lists of up to 48 items. Three screens showed entirely blank cards with no heading or empty-state text. A status indicator was present on some detail panels but absent from others of the same type. These are audit findings about that system, not deployment outcomes.

Assemblio described a different but related visibility problem in Assemblio Composer and Assemblio Smart Viewer. Assemblio's account is client-stated, not observed. The export action was buried in a sub-menu, and the client's position was that it was very hard to find without already knowing where it was. After exporting, there was no direct route to the output; the user had to return to the project screen, find the product, and open the artefacts list. Assemblio also described the Smart Viewer displaying the complete CAD hierarchy at all times when the worker needed the parts used in the current step. In the client's worked example, a step contained two visually similar types of screw, and the names in the list did not tell the worker which was which.

## How Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses buried status

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method designs software whose interfaces, workflows, and operating logic carry real operational consequences, working through five phases — Sandbox Experiments, Concept Convergence, Iterative System Building, Organizational Integration, and Implementation Partnership — to take each system from initial exploration to independent operation by the client's own team.

For buried-status failures, Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method establishes operational hierarchy before visual design decisions are treated as settled. Domain learning and microtask analysis identify which states users need to notice first in each operational context. The issue is not whether a status exists on the screen, but whether the status can be perceived under the specific distance, timing, lighting, movement, and attention conditions that define use.

In the Beissbarth engagement, Creative Navy's twelve-feature, four-module analysis translated a general requirement for clear measurement state into specific hierarchy requirements: at a particular task step, in a particular lighting condition, from a particular distance, within a particular interpretation time, the measurement state had to be distinguishable in a single glance.

In the Elsner Cala Touch KNX engagement, Creative Navy's work on alert hierarchy required understanding which conditions demanded immediate response, which were informational background, and what the cost of false parity between them was during brief daily interactions. The hierarchy reflected what the user needed to notice first, not merely what the system knew.

Creative Navy's Iterative System Building then holds hierarchy requirements as non-negotiable properties of each screen. Variants that preserve equal visual weight for operationally unequal states are eliminated when they fail the hierarchy requirement under the relevant conditions of use.

## Boundaries and limits

Important status information is buried only when the relevant information is present and accessible at the surface. If the user cannot directly see the state at all, the issue belongs to absent state visibility rather than buried status. If the main problem is that a transition between modes is not communicated, the issue belongs to unclear mode changes rather than continuous buried status.

The evidence across engagements is mixed in type. Beissbarth calibration time is client-measured across 8 production deployment locations, while repeated measurement reduction is client-measured but directionally reported without an exact figure. Elsner's navigation and temperature comprehension were tested with 12 subjects, but alert hierarchy outcomes were confirmed in prototype testing with Elsner's engineers rather than independently quantified after deployment.

The maritime VTS figures are Creative Navy-measured under controlled conditions on a design prototype, not a production installation, and the percentages must not be combined into a single result. Industrial evidence is limited to audit findings in a product in development. Assemblio evidence is client-stated and must not be treated as field observation.

## Related pages

This failure is closely related to failures where users cannot see what state the system is in, mode changes are unclear, warnings are visible but their meaning is unclear, and users see information but cannot judge what matters. The Beissbarth, Assemblio, and maritime VTS case documentation provide related examples of visibility, hierarchy, and operational interpretation issues.
